articles.title: US, Israel prepare for fresh Iran strikes after midterms as Tehran threatens with ‘Father of All Bombs’
articles.summary: The United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed military strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, according to a report by The New
articles.body: The United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed military strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, according to a report by The New York Times.Meanwhile, Tehran has threatened to unveil a weapon it calls the “Father of All Bombs” amid escalating tensions in West Asia.The proposed US-Israeli operation could involve a short but intensive campaign targeting Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenal.Citing US officials and others briefed on the deliberations, The New York Times reported that the two militaries had stepped up exercises, including flights over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres.US war secretary Pete Hegseth also met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss the possibility of renewed strikes, according to the report.Some US officials believe another round of attacks could push Iran's economy to the brink and pressure Tehran into making diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.However, it remains uncertain whether US President Donald Trump will approve a fresh operation.A White House official said the administration did not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist”, adding that Trump was keeping all options on the table to ensure Iran could not acquire nuclear weapons.Iran threatens to unveil ‘Father of All Bombs’Amid reports of possible renewed strikes, Iran has warned that it would respond to any fresh military action.Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said Iran was preparing to unveil a weapon described as the “Father of All Bombs”, according to statements carried by Iranian media outlets.“The United States has the ‘Mother of All Bombs.’ We will show them the ‘Father of All Bombs,’ and it will definitely be something new for them,” Mohebbi said, according to Iran's Student News Network (SNN).In separate remarks carried by Iran's Young Journalists Club news agency, Mohebbi said, “We are in the stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs.’ This is something new for the enemy.”He did not provide details about the weapon or explain its capabilities.Mohebbi also said Iran's missile stockpile had increased 1.5 times following the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, without providing specific figures. He claimed that missile quality, range, destructive power and accuracy had improved significantly.The IRGC spokesperson said Iran was moving towards a defence doctrine based on permanent deterrence and asymmetric warfare.“Now, we say that if a country attacks us, we will not only respond but also launch an offensive,” he said.“Our doctrine will no longer be merely offensive; it will be asymmetric. We will attack the enemy in a way that makes them feel the intensity of our response,” Mohebbi added.Questions over possible use of ‘Mother of All Bombs’The Iranian threat follows reports that Trump has considered using the US GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “Mother of All Bombs”, against Iran's deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.The conventional bomb weighs approximately 9,800 kg (21,600 pounds) and is among the largest non-nuclear weapons in the US arsenal. Trump authorised its first use during his initial presidential term, when it was deployed against an Islamic State tunnel complex in Afghanistan in April 2017.However, weapons specialists have questioned whether the bomb could destroy Iran's underground nuclear facility, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite.The MOAB explodes above ground rather than functioning as a deep-penetration weapon. Military officials have also raised concerns about its delivery, as the bomb would have to be carried by a relatively slow-flying MC-130 transport aircraft that could be vulnerable to Iranian anti-aircraft fire.A separate report by CNN last week said US military planners had developed strike options that included the potential use of the MOAB against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.The report also highlighted doubts over whether the weapon could penetrate deeply enough to destroy heavily fortified underground facilities.The bomb could cause extensive destruction at the surface but might not achieve the intended military objectives against deeply buried targets.US builds up military presence as diplomatic efforts continueAccording to The New York Times, the United States is assembling a substantial military force expected to be fully in place by early November. The planned deployment includes three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces.The report said political considerations, including Trump's earlier pledge not to launch strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, could affect the timing of any operation.The US and Israel reportedly came close to launching another attack earlier this month, but Trump postponed the operation shortly before it was due to begin, despite extensive preparations and heightened alert levels among their air forces.Washington is also seeking to use the threat of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme and control of the Strait of Hormuz, the report said.Iranian negotiators, however, have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that it be addressed later in the talks.Some US planners believe a three-day campaign could inflict enough economic damage to change Tehran's position.However, previous US-Israeli strikes between February and April drove up energy prices and inflation worldwide, affected security across West Asia and severely strained the Pentagon's supply of missile interceptors, according to the report.Iranian officials have warned that any renewed conflict could extend beyond commercial shipping and energy infrastructure to data centres and underwater internet cables.Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran's negotiator General Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, rejected the prospect of a swift end to renewed hostilities.Describing the idea that the US could conclude another round of strikes within 72 hours as a “fantasy”, Mohammadi said Iran would determine when the war would end.“Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” he said. “We are determined and confident and strong planning has been put in place.”Pezeshkian says Iran faces a ‘super-challenge’Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has described the situation as a major challenge for Tehran.Addressing the Iranian Parliament, Pezeshkian said, “The memorandum of understanding we signed was very good; we hadn't given anything. The current situation is neither good for us, nor for the region, nor for the world.”He added, “We are in a super-challenge, not a challenge. America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm.”Iran's representative to the United Nations also alleged, according to SNN, that Starlink had been used to identify and target locations in military attacks against Iran, adding that the country's space and scientific infrastructure had come under attack.The timing of any renewed operation could also be affected by Israel's October 27 election.Analysts believe Netanyahu could face difficulties initiating a war if he loses and becomes a caretaker prime minister.Others believe the prospect of joint US-Israeli strikes could be used to pressure political rivals into joining a unity government.With military preparations continuing and negotiations yet to produce a breakthrough, uncertainty remains over Trump's decision and the scale of Iran's potential response.You use AI every day. articles.summary: US vice president JD Vance has voiced support for Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy amid backlash over a campaign advertisement
articles.body: US vice president JD Vance has voiced support for Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy amid backlash over a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. Calling himself “disgusted” by fellow Republicans’ criticism, Vance urged them to focus on winning elections rather than objecting to the controversial ad.Speaking at a campaign rally near Cincinnati on Wednesday, Vance said he was “a little bit disgusted” by Republicans criticising the advertisement, which features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying and questioning her suitability for office.“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said, in his first public comments on the controversy.According to news agency AP, Vance accused Democrats of using political tactics against Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former Republican presidential candidate, saying they had “throw[n] every dirty trick in the political book at Vivek”, including calling him a “murderer”, while “the whole time Vivek has stood tall and talked about what he wants to accomplish.”“The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because — guess what? — Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” he said.“My message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days,” Vance added.The 60-second advertisement has drawn criticism from both parties. According to AP, Arthur lost custody of her children after her second husband was indicted for raping Acton, who has said she has not seen her mother since 1978, when she was 12.“I won't normalise somebody who has said that my childhood is ‘something I'm just complaining about’, who today, just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect and sexual abuse,” Acton told HQ News Now.Republican senator Jon Husted, who is running against former senator Sherrod Brown, said he would not have run the advertisement. Former South Carolina governor Nikki Haley called Ramaswamy “a bad guy”, while Meghan McCain also criticised the spot, AP reported.US president Donald Trump had earlier told reporters he knew nothing about the advertisement but said he had heard “the mother went very rogue on the daughter”. He added: “I don’t think that has anything to do with Vivek.”Despite the backlash, Ramaswamy’s campaign plans to spend $4 million airing the advertisement on television and online. Acton’s campaign has released a separate advertisement urging voters to “find more breathing room, and let's heal what has divided us”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: How Denmark restored 26 kilometres of the Skjern River and returned 2,200 hectares of farmland to marshland, bringing wildlife back
articles.summary: In western Jutland, Denmark chose to undo an engineering project and give one of its largest rivers back its natural course.
articles.body: In western Jutland, Denmark chose to undo an engineering project and give one of its largest rivers back its natural course. The Skjern River had been straightened and embanked so that surrounding marshland could be farmed. Today, 26 kilometres of the river meander again, around 2,200 hectares have returned to marshland, and wildlife has come back in significant numbers. Here’s why the original farming scheme faltered, what the restoration involved, how communities, farmers and visitors have gained, and why the project matters for other regions weighing the cost of restoring nature against the cost of leaving it damaged.Why straightening the Skjern River and farming its marshland in western Jutland stopped paying offThe story begins in the 1960s, when a major project set out to straighten and embank the Skjern River, one of the largest in Denmark, and turn the surrounding marshland into agricultural land. For a while the gamble appeared to work, because the first crops grown on the reclaimed ground were fairly successful. The trouble came with time. According to the European Commission, productivity on the land diminished drastically, even though farmers applied large amounts of fertiliser to keep yields up. By 1987, the result was a stretch of low-quality farmland, and the government launched a major restoration project in response. In effect, the project that had treated marshland as land to be converted to farming was replaced by one that treated it as an asset to be recovered.Reshaping 26 kilometres of the Skjern River into a meandering bed and returning 2,200 hectares to marshlandThe restoration launched in 1987 was, in essence, the 1960s project played in reverse. Rather than leaving the river confined to a straightened and embanked channel, the government had the Skjern River re-excavated and placed into a more natural, meandering riverbed. That new course stretches over 26 kilometres. Alongside the river itself, the project reconverted around 2,200 hectares of surrounding land to marshland, an area equal to roughly 22 square kilometres. This land had been turned over to agriculture in the 1960s, so the work meant giving up farmland that had already proved disappointing. In practical terms, ground that once received large amounts of fertiliser is now marshland. Taken together, the changes did not simply tidy up a damaged river. They rebuilt the wider landscape of river and marshland that the original scheme had removed.Better water quality, returning wildlife and up to 400,000 visitors on the new Skjern River nature trailsThe ecological response was swift. Water quality improved quickly, and wildlife came back in significant numbers. That is a notable turnaround for land that had been farmed with large amounts of fertiliser to little lasting effect. The restored marshland also became a magnet for people in search of nature. By the end of the project, some 350,000 to 400,000 people were using the new nature trails, a figure that shows how strongly the public responded to a landscape reshaped for recovery rather than production. The trails turned an environmental repair job into a destination, giving visitors a reason to walk through land that had once been given over to farming. The site is now valued for its water, its wildlife and its walking routes rather than for the crops it was once expected to grow.Farming support and a cost-benefit analysis showing local economic opportunities outweighed project costsFarmers were not overlooked. They were given support to adopt more nature-friendly farming practices, which paired the return of marshland with help for the people who work the land. A cost-benefit analysis of the restoration then concluded that the local economic opportunities it created were larger than the overall project cost. The European Commission's collection of nature restoration success stories points to a similar result elsewhere. In Belgium, a social cost-benefit analysis behind the Sigma Plan II, a long-term flood protection and nature restoration strategy on the edge of Antwerp, found that improving natural infrastructure is cheaper than constructing and maintaining a storm surge barrier near the city. Read together, the Danish and Belgian examples suggest that restoring ecosystems can make economic sense as well as environmental sense.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: A miniature wooden pagoda commissioned by a Japanese empress around 770 CE has sold for $40,960 at Christie's, fetching nearly 2.8 times its highest estimate. The object, which contains an ancient printed Buddhist prayer, offers a glimpse into an early chapter of printing history.A wooden pagoda small enough to hold in one's hands has survived for more than 1,250 years, carrying within it a printed Buddhist prayer from eighth-century Japan. The historic object has now attracted a substantial sum at auction, selling for $40,960 against an estimate of $10,000 to $15,000.The object, known as a Hyakumanto pagoda with printed dharani, was offered by Christie's in its Fine Printed Books, Manuscripts, and Science sale. According to the auction house's catalogue, it dates to Japan's Nara Period, around 770 CE, and is associated with an extraordinary royal commission: the production of one million miniature pagodas by Empress Shotoku.The sale price was nearly 2.8 times the upper end of the estimate, reflecting the historical significance of an object that brings together religious devotion, early printing and an ambitious project commissioned more than a millennium ago.The story behind Japan's million miniature pagodasAccording to Christie’s, the pagoda belongs to a series known as Hyakumanto, a Japanese term referring to one million pagodas. Empress Shotoku commissioned the miniature wooden structures during the eighth century, with the intention of distributing them among Buddhist temples across Japan.Historical accounts associate the commission with the suppression of a rebellion in 764 CE and the empress's prayers for the protection of the realm. Christie's notes that accounts of the commission's motivation vary, but the project was rooted in Buddhist religious practice.Each pagoda was designed to house a small scroll called a dharani - a Buddhist charm or invocation. These prayers were printed on paper and placed inside a hollow cavity in the wooden structure.The prayers were associated with the Buddhist belief that religious merit could be gained through practices such as copying sacred texts and constructing repositories for them. The commission therefore served a religious purpose while also representing a remarkable undertaking in the production of printed material.The scale of the project was striking for its time. Rather than commissioning a single sacred object, the empress ordered a vast series of miniature pagodas, each containing a printed prayer.What makes this tiny pagoda historically significant?The example sold at Christie's is a three-tier wooden pagoda measuring 212 mm, or about 21.2 cm, in height. It has a detachable finial, which covers the cavity containing the printed prayer, and comes with a fitted, inscribed wooden box.The accompanying dharani features a standard layout of 31 columns, with five characters in each column. Christie's catalogue notes that the text has some old restoration, mainly around the margins, affecting about ten characters.Its significance extends beyond its age. Christie's describes the object as an example of the earliest authenticated physical printing, while acknowledging a competing claim from Korea. The precise printing method used for the prayers remains uncertain: historians have debated whether they were produced using woodblocks or metal plates.The pagodas are associated with some of the earliest reliably dated examples of printing. They predate Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing in Europe by several centuries. However, they should not be described as definitively the world's oldest printed material, since earlier examples have been identified or proposed elsewhere in East Asia.A religious project that became part of printing historyThe Hyakumanto commission reflects the role Buddhism played in the development and use of early printing in East Asia. Printed texts were often produced for religious and ritual purposes, rather than primarily for reading in the modern sense.An educational resource developed by Keio University on the history of Japanese books and printing explains that early printed texts were used in religious rites and valued for their symbolic and ritual significance.The prayers inside the pagodas were based on Buddhist scripture. Their purpose was linked to religious merit and spiritual protection, making the objects both devotional offerings and carefully produced containers for sacred texts.The project also demonstrates the scale at which printing could be organised in eighth-century Japan. Producing a million miniature pagodas and their associated prayers required a substantial coordinated effort, long before printing transformed the production and circulation of books in Europe.From an eighth-century commission to a modern auctionThe pagoda's recent sale brings renewed attention to an object that connects religious history with the evolution of printing. While its exact journey across the centuries cannot be established from the available catalogue information alone, Christie's records an earlier appearance at its New York auction on June 12, 2015, as lot 49.The object was subsequently offered in the auction house's Fine Printed Books, Manuscripts, and Science sale, which closed on October 13, 2026. It realised $40,960 against an estimate of $10,000 to $15,000.The result was nearly 2.8 times the upper estimate and more than four times the lower estimate. Christie's states that estimates exclude the buyer's premium and applicable taxes, so the reported result should not automatically be interpreted as the buyer's total cost.More than 1,250 years after it was made, the miniature pagoda remains a tangible link to a period when printing was already being used to reproduce religious texts on a remarkable scale. Its significance lies not only in the price it achieved, but also in what it preserves: evidence of an early printing tradition, a major Buddhist commission and the enduring relationship between technology and religious practice.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, Emma Stone paid $2.3 million for a 1926 Los Angeles home, renovated it and added a guesthouse; five years later, the property sold for $4.3 million, more than $300,000 above its asking price
articles.summary: A nearly century-old Los Angeles home turned into a profitable real estate deal for actor Emma Stone after she bought the property for $2.3 million,
articles.body: A nearly century-old Los Angeles home turned into a profitable real estate deal for actor Emma Stone after she bought the property for $2.3 million, renovated it and added a separate guesthouse. According to Realtor.com’s February 2024 report, the Spanish-style home sold for $4.3 million, fetching $305,000 more than its asking price of $3.995 million. The sale came just weeks after the property was listed, following a renovation that blended its original architectural features with updated interiors.Stone purchased the two-storey property in 2019 in the Comstock Hills area of Westwood, Los Angeles. Built in 1926, the house spans approximately 3,276 square feet and has four bedrooms and four bathrooms. The gated residence was listed for sale in January 2024, with the listing handled by Eric Lavey of Sotheby’s International Realty. Architectural Digest reported on January 24 that the home had found a buyer in less than 10 days, although the contract price had not been disclosed at the time. Realtor.com subsequently reported the final $4.3 million sale price.The transaction represented a $2 million increase over the original purchase price. However, that difference is the gap between the reported purchase and sale prices, not a confirmed profit: the available reports do not establish the total renovation expenditure, transaction costs, taxes or other expenses associated with the property.Renovation preserved the home’s Spanish-style characterStone’s renovation focused on expanding and updating the home while retaining features that reflected its 1920s origins. According to Architectural Digest and Inman, the actor expanded the kitchen and added a detached guesthouse to the property. The changes created additional living space while preserving some of the original architectural details.The home’s design combines Spanish Colonial influences with colourful, contemporary touches. Its exterior features a cream-coloured facade, pale green gate and matching shutters, with a terracotta-toned walkway leading towards the entrance. The property also has a landscaped front yard and a spacious backyard, giving the residence a cottage-like appearance despite its location in Los Angeles.Inside, the house has a curved staircase, hardwood floors, arched doorways and exposed wooden beams. The living room includes a fireplace, built-in shelving and a distinctive ceiling with colourful detailing. These features help retain the character of an older home while allowing for a more contemporary interior.The kitchen became one of the property’s standout spaces after the renovation. It features white cabinetry, a farmhouse-style sink, a colourful turquoise range and double-height vaulted ceilings that allow natural light into the room. A separate sitting nook provides additional space beside the kitchen, connecting the cooking and living areas.Other details include a tiled courtyard, a balcony overlooking the outdoor area and a bathroom fitted with a claw-foot bathtub. The interiors also incorporate patterned wallpaper, colourful furnishings and decorative artwork, giving the house a more individual style than a conventional neutral-toned luxury listing.Detached guesthouse adds another dimensionBeyond the main residence, the property includes a detached guesthouse that was added as part of the renovation. According to the listing details reported by Realtor.com, the additional structure has its own living room and kitchen, a separate bedroom suite and laundry facilities. It can accommodate visiting family and friends or potentially serve as an independent workspace.The guesthouse effectively gives the property two distinct living spaces. Rather than simply adding another bedroom to the main house, the separate structure offers greater privacy for occupants and flexibility in how the property can be used. Together with the main home and outdoor areas, it helped position the residence as a small compound rather than a standalone cottage.The home’s location was another feature highlighted in property reports. Situated in the Comstock Hills area of Westwood, it is near the Los Angeles Country Club and a short drive from the University of California, Los Angeles. The gated setting, outdoor space and proximity to established Los Angeles neighbourhoods were among the features described in the listing coverage.A quick sale at a premiumThe speed of the transaction was notable. Stone’s property was listed for $3.995 million in January 2024, and Architectural Digest reported that it had secured a buyer in under 10 days. At that stage, the contract price had not been made public. The final sale was subsequently reported at $4.3 million in February, confirming that the property had sold above its original asking price.The final price was approximately 7.6% above the asking price. It was also nearly 87% higher than the $2.3 million Stone had paid in 2019, based on the two reported transaction prices. These comparisons describe the increase in the home’s market price, rather than Stone’s net return after expenses.The sale was part of a wider history of property transactions involving the actor. Architectural Digest reported in 2019 that Stone had acquired two Los Angeles-area homes that year: the Westwood property for $2.3 million and a separate midcentury house in Malibu for approximately $3.25 million. The Malibu property was later sold in 2022 for about $4.425 million, according to House Beautiful’s account of her real estate portfolio.The Westwood sale illustrates how renovations can change the appeal of an older property by combining period architecture with additional living space and updated amenities. In Stone’s case, the 1926 house retained its arched doorways, exposed beams and tiled courtyard, while the expanded kitchen and detached guesthouse added functionality. Its $4.3 million sale in 2024 closed the chapter on a property that had spent nearly five years in her real estate portfolio.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision?
